title: Friday, Which Friday?
focus: 确认日期、时区和演示用途
story:
On Thursday afternoon, an invitation arrives with the title 'Friday demo'. I open it while waiting for a test to finish. It shows a time in the late afternoon, so I accept and return to my code.

Five minutes later, Daniel sends a message: 'Need the version ready by Friday morning.'

I type 'Sure'. Before I send it, I look again at the invitation. It has no explanation of what ready means. The meeting includes Elena in London and several people I have never met.

Friday morning where?

I delete my answer and walk to Daniel's desk. He is speaking into his headset, drawing circles in the air with one finger. I wait at a distance until he looks up.

“Two minutes,” he says, covering the microphone.

I point at the small kitchen and go to fill my water bottle. The machine makes a long noise before giving me half a cup. By the time I return, Daniel has ended his call.

“About Friday morning,” I say. “Do you mean Shanghai time or London time?”

“London. Elena wants to check the demonstration before the staff session.”

“So there are two sessions?”

He looks at his calendar. “You've only got the second invitation?”

I show him my screen.

“Right. I missed you off the first.”

For a moment I feel pleased that the confusion is not entirely mine. Then he opens another message, and I notice a different date.

“This says next Friday,” I say.

“That's the staff session. The check with Elena is tomorrow.”

I sit in the empty chair beside him. “Could we put both dates and both time zones in one message?”

Daniel rubs his eyes. “Please do. Send it to me before it goes out.”

At my desk, I open the calendar's world clock rather than calculate from memory. The London offset changes during the year, and I do not want yesterday's guess to become today's appointment. For these dates, the calendar shows London eight hours behind Shanghai.

I write two lines. The first is a short check with Elena this Friday at nine in the morning London time, five in the afternoon Shanghai time. The second is the staff demonstration on the following Friday, at the same local times. I include the full calendar date on each line.

Then I add a third sentence: 'Both sessions use the test environment and test learner accounts.'

Rui reads it over my shoulder.

“Add that neither session is a launch.”

“Would anyone think that?”

“Someone wrote 'ready Friday'. Someone else might forward it.”

I add the sentence. Daniel approves the message and corrects both invitations. Elena replies with a thank-you and one question: can staff try changing a class themselves during the second session?

That question changes our preparation. A demonstration I control is different from six people clicking buttons. Rui and I book time to reset the test classes, check permissions and prepare separate accounts.

We also choose one sample class to use if the system is slow. Daniel asks whether we need a recording as a backup.

“A few screenshots would be quicker,” I say. “They can explain the steps, but they won't prove the live test is working.”

“Fine. Label them clearly.”

By Friday afternoon, the screenshots are ready. So are the test accounts. I join the call ten minutes early and discover that I cannot share the application window. I leave and rejoin after changing a permission, grateful that Elena is not yet waiting.

At five, her face appears.

“Good morning,” I say, then laugh. “Your morning.”

“Good afternoon to you. Shall we start with what staff will see?”

We change a test class from ten to eleven. The notification arrives in a test inbox. Elena reads it silently.

“Could the old time be easier to notice?” she asks.

I write that down. We have time to adjust the layout before the staff demonstration. We do not have to pretend the first version is final.

When the call ends, Daniel asks if I can stay late next Friday in case the staff session runs over.

“I can stay until six,” I say. “After that, I have an appointment.”

“Rui?” Daniel asks.

“I'm helping my family on Friday evening. I have to leave at six too.”

Daniel studies the invitation again. “I thought I had the two of you until the end.”

“You have both of us until six,” Rui says. “What do you actually need at the end?”

Daniel counts on his fingers. He wants people to change a class, read the message, and talk about what to do if a learner calls. The last part is where he expects difficult questions. If he leaves it to the end, the people he wants in the room may already be on the train.

“Then why save it for last?” I ask.

“Because it's the conversation I can't put a time on,” he says. He looks down at his fingers. “Which is an excellent reason to start it earlier.”

He moves the support discussion earlier.

On the train home, my phone shows the two invitations beside each other. Same title, different dates, clear descriptions. I close the calendar and send Maya a message that I will be home for dinner.

The following Friday, a woman at one of the centre desks changes the time of a test class. Then she pushes her chair away from the screen.

“Pretend the phone has just rung,” she says.

A man beside her picks up a folded sheet of paper and holds it to his ear. He does such a good front-desk voice that someone at the other end of the call tries to answer him.

When she comes back, she finds the new time easily. What she wants next is the list of people who should hear about it. We can show her test names. She recognises none of them, of course, and she laughs at herself for trying.

“Next time,” she says, “could you show us how you know you have the right list?”

It's a fair question. We have made these accounts ourselves. There is a whole step between a list we wrote and a list held by the centre.

At six Rui stands up with his coat on. My hand is already on the lid of my laptop. Daniel catches my eye and points at the door. He stays to collect the final questions. This time the invitation has been right about the end as well as the beginning.

phrases.en: Which time zone do you mean?
Do you mean this Friday or next Friday?

phrases.zh: 汇总两个日期以供核对

phrases.en: This is a demonstration, not a launch.

phrases.zh: 说明可用时间的截止点

practice.grammar: 用 this 与 next 明确相对日期，再用完整日期确认：Do you mean this Friday or next Friday? 相对日期可能含糊，实际沟通时补上日历日期和时区。
practice.pronunciation: 读出并区分：THIS Friday / NEXT Friday；nine in LONDON / five in SHANGHAI。先重读变化词，再把两组放入完整确认句中。

questions.q: Why does Andy first think there is only one session?
questions.a: He has received only the invitation for the staff demonstration.

questions.q: Why do they move the support discussion earlier?
questions.a: Andy and Rui both have to leave at six, and staff may need them for that discussion.

questions.q: What does Elena ask Andy to change after the check?
questions.a: She asks him to make the old class time easier to notice.

roleplay.context: 你是 Andy，收到了两个容易混淆的会议安排，需要逐项核对。

turns.line: We need it ready Friday morning.
turns.cue: 问清是哪一个周五以及哪个时区。

turns.line: The client check is tomorrow; the staff session is next week.
turns.cue: 复述两个安排，并说明会发送含完整日期的确认。

turns.line: Can you stay as late as needed?
turns.cue: 给出可留到的时间，并建议提前安排必要讨论。

practice.transfer: 你与国外朋友约一次视频通话。用英语确认日期、双方本地时间和预计时长，最后完整复述安排；使用实际日历核对。
practice.retell: 用一至两分钟讲清两个会议如何被混淆和纠正。结尾说明为什么测试账号与“不是上线”这两点需要写进邀请。
